questions.stem: State the bookkeeping rule that connects energy transferred with work done.
questions.modelAnswer: The energy transferred is equal to the work done, as demanded by conservation of energy.

questions.stem: Explain why a swinging pendulum never climbs higher than its starting height in an idealised model.
questions.modelAnswer: With conservation of energy and a perfect transfer, all the gravitational potential energy at the top of one swing becomes kinetic energy at the bottom and back again. No energy leaks away, so the gravitational store can never exceed its starting value and the swing height repeats exactly.

questions.stem: A child's swing reaches the same height on every push while friction stays negligible. Name the two stores taking turns to hold the energy.
questions.modelAnswer: The energy alternates between the swing's gravitational potential store at the top of each arc and its kinetic store at the bottom, with conservation of energy keeping the total fixed.

questions.stem: State the assumption hidden in the phrase perfect energy transfer.
questions.modelAnswer: No energy is wasted or dissipated, so the entire amount leaving one store arrives in the next.

questions.stem: State the equating rule used for a perfect fall.
questions.modelAnswer: The decrease in gravitational potential energy equals the increase in kinetic energy, so the two store changes can be set equal.

questions.stem: Explain why ignoring resistance is a modelling choice rather than a claim about the real world.
questions.modelAnswer: Every real transfer leaks some energy to the thermal stores of the surroundings, so a perfect transfer never actually happens. The assumption is adopted only because the question declares wasted transfers negligible, making the store arithmetic tractable.

questions.stem: A 50 kg sledder starts from rest and descends an 8 m slope in a perfect transfer (g = 10 N/kg). Calculate the sledder's speed at the bottom.
questions.modelAnswer: Gravitational energy released = 50 × 10 × 8 = 4000 J; equating the kinetic store gives v = √(2 × 4000 ÷ 50) = √160, so the speed at the bottom is about 13 m/s.
